concepts.definition: The piece a model uses when it processes text; it can be a word, part of a word, a letter or punctuation.
concepts.example: In the tool, `robotlar` (robots) is split into three tokens: `▁robot`, `l`, `ar`.
concepts.pitfall: Treating the token count as equal to the word count; a token is often smaller than a word.

concepts.definition: The whole number that matches each token; the model processes text as this sequence of numbers.
concepts.example: To the model, the sequence [▁robot] [l] [ar] is a list of three whole numbers.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking the model reads letters and words directly.

concepts.definition: In the tool, the number of learned merge steps the tokeniser applies; as it rises, the token count falls.
concepts.example: `robot ileri` (robot forward) takes 12 tokens with 0 merges and 2 tokens with many merges.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking the token count at zero merges is just the number of letters; the start-of-word mark counts as a token too.

concepts.definition: A mark showing that a piece is at the start of a word; in the tool it also appears as "·".
concepts.example: "▁robot" is a separate word, while "robot" is a piece coming from inside another word.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking the mark is a space character and leaving it out of the token count.

concepts.definition: A collection of text used to train a tokeniser or a model.
concepts.example: The tool has two small corpora, one Turkish and one English.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking the tool's tokeniser, trained on a small corpus, is a real model's.

concepts.definition: The same text in a language seen less in training is split into more, smaller tokens.
concepts.example: With 120 merges, "the robot turns left" takes 4 tokens with the English corpus and 13 with the Turkish corpus.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking more tokens means "richer" meaning; it only means the tokeniser fits that language poorly.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is true about tokens?
options: Every token is a whole word
A token can also be part of a word, a letter or punctuation
A token is made only of numbers
A token is the full stop at the end of a sentence
quiz.explanation: A token can be a whole word, but it can also be part of a word, a single letter or punctuation. That is why the first option is wrong; inside the model tokens are turned into numbers, but a token itself is not just a number.

quiz.prompt: In the tool, with the number of merges at 0, you typed "robot ileri". Each letter is a separate token, and the mark at the start of each word is a separate token too. How many tokens appear in total?
quiz.explanation: "robot" is 5 letters plus 1 start-of-word mark, so 6 tokens; "ileri" is also 5 letters plus 1 mark, 6 tokens. Total 6 + 6 = 12. People who count only the letters get 10 and forget the mark.

quiz.prompt:
The tokeniser split the word "robotlar" into three tokens. What does this code print when it runs?

```
const parcalar = ["▁robot", "l", "ar"]
console.log(parcalar.length)
console.log(parcalar.join("").replace("▁", ""))
```
quiz.explanation: The array has three elements, so the first line prints 3. join joins the pieces with no spaces between them, and replace deletes the start-of-word mark; the result is robotlar. Splitting into pieces does not lose information: when you join the pieces, the text comes back.

quiz.prompt:
A student wants to find how many tokens a sentence will take up in the model. There is one bug in the code; which is it?

```
const cumle = "robotlar duvarı görünce durur"
const tokenSayisi = cumle.split(" ").length
console.log("Model " + tokenSayisi + " token görür")
```
options: The cumle variable should not be const
split(" ") counts words; it assumes the token count is the same as the word count
The + sign cannot be used in the console.log call
The sentence has no full stop
quiz.explanation: split(" ") counts the words and finds 4. But "robotlar" on its own can be more than one token; the token count can only be found by running the tokeniser. Using const and joining text with + are not problems in this code.

quiz.prompt: The same English sentence takes far more tokens with a tokeniser trained on the Turkish corpus (13 tokens) than with one trained on the English corpus (4 tokens). What is the most likely reason?
options: A tokeniser splits a language it saw less in training into smaller pieces
The Turkish corpus contains a bigger vocabulary
quiz.explanation: A tokeniser makes the pieces it sees often into single tokens; a language it saw less in training does not have these pieces, so the text breaks into small pieces close to single letters. The calculation is not random; it gives the same result every time.
